Title: To scale Gen AI, should we focus on compute or memory - Community - OpenAI Developer Community
# To scale Gen AI, should we focus on compute or memory. Most of the focus now is on compute for Generative AI. But I see we should focus more on memory architecture than compute. To build a memory system, I think the best tool is to use a graph db. Great point on focusing on memory architecture, akin to the human brain’s efficiency. I sit in the camp of the future of generative AI, and solving scalability issues, hinges on a blend of approaches and there won’t be one solution that rules them all. Techniques like FSDP and QLoRA, as explored in a recent deep dive (Answer.AI - Enabling 70B Finetuning on Consumer GPUs), further highlight the potential for balancing compute and memory effectively. Scaling a pretrained transformer LLM and calling it “AI” is like in 1880 saying that what we need is ever bigger steam engines. What we actually needed was an advancement in technology, like the internal combustion engine. And now, what we need is something closer to actual artificial intelligence, which these pretrained models are not, at ll. It’s good to keep expanding what these can do, but it isn’t AI, and it’s no more a long-term solution for AI than moving from steam engines to diesel-electric locomotives was for human transportation. The focus on this flashy, but unintelligent kind of model has distracted us from REAL progress in actual intelligence. So what we really need is to work on dynamic learning, instead of pretrained models, and even among pretrained models we need to work on advancing the technology, for example to solve the need to tokenize more than language, so that the transformer can “understand” information in other formats better than the LLM can kluge “music” and “images” post-training. This isn’t AI science, it’s pretrained model engineering. This isn’t AI science, it’s pretrained model engineering. Even as other architectures unfold, it’s important to actually create something *useful*, which is what we have with “pretrained model engineering”. So we need researchers to formulate new ideas and approaches, engineers that design and build these things and get them to work, and marketers that get people to fork over their money.

results.title: Verdict: Scaling Judge-Time Compute | Leonard Tang
results.content: When multiple users trigger concurrent generations, you need to handle: – Async execution – Retries + failures – Credit tracking – Worker stability That’s where Celery + Redis save your system: - Redis Queue: Manages async workloads — no blocked threads, no timeouts - Celery Workers: Scale horizontally when demand spikes - Atomic Updates: Concurrency-safe credit + DB ops - Caching: Stops duplicate LLM calls, saves $$, and compute Once this pipeline clicks: - Backend breathes - Costs drop - Users stay happy Scaling AI isn’t about bigger models - it’s about smarter pipelines.

results.title: Beyond Memorization: Extending Reasoning Depth with Recurrence, Memory and Test-Time Compute Scaling | by Sai Dheeraj Gummadi | Medium
results.content: # Beyond Memorization: Extending Reasoning Depth with Recurrence, Memory and Test-Time Compute Scaling. The paper shows that increasing a model’s effective depth at inference via recurrence, external memory, and test-time compute scaling substantially improves multi-step reasoning on tasks designed to prevent rote memorization, highlighting depth and iterative computation as central levers beyond larger parameter counts or longer chain-of-thought. Reasoning performance in LLMs often collapses as problems require many sequential updates, and standard training/evaluation setups can confound “understanding” with memorization of common patterns; this work isolates genuine reasoning by using cellular automata with random Boolean rules and random initial conditions, then asks how architectural choices and inference-time compute affect multi-step rollouts. * Recurrence and memory extend effective depth: Allowing recurrent processing and providing memory mechanisms significantly extend the “effective depth” at test time, closing much of the gap on multi-step tasks without changing parameter count. * Test-time compute scaling helps: Scaling computation during inference — by iterating recurrent blocks more times or leveraging memory — substantially boosts long-horizon reasoning, aligning with broader evidence that compute-at-inference can be more efficient than always scaling parameters. The results tie into a growing line of work that scales inference-time compute via latent recurrence rather than token-length chain-of-thought, allowing models to “think” internally at test time by unrolling recurrent blocks to variable depth depending on problem difficulty. External or persistent memory provides state across recurrent steps, stabilizing longer computations; in the paper’s controlled setting, memory plus recurrence further improves multi-step accuracy, suggesting design patterns where memory slots or scratchpads become first-class citizens of inference. * Product strategy: For reasoning-heavy use cases (math, planning, theorem-like tasks), add a latent “deliberation” budget — iterate recurrent layers more on hard prompts or enable an external memory — to trade compute for quality adaptively. * Recurrent latent reasoning and continuous depth at test time, allowing arbitrary unrolling and adaptive compute. By constructing a regime that rules out rote memorization and then showing that recurrence, memory, and test-time compute scaling extend a model’s effective reasoning depth, this work provides clean evidence for investing in latent, iterative inference as a first-class design axis for next-generation reasoning systems.

results.title: Training at Scale: Chinchilla Scaling Laws for Compute-Optimal Training of LLMs | by Zain ul Abideen | Medium
results.content: In this blog post, I will be discussing a paper from Google DeepMind in which they perform a lot of experiments on training large language models to find the relation between model size, compute budget, and no. The authors mention that for compute-optimal training, the number of training tokens and model size must be scaled equally. Using power law, they found out that the optimal model size for Gopher’s compute budget (5.76 × 10^23) is 67B and training tokens should be 1.5 trillion. This approach suggests that the optimal model size for Gopher’s compute budget is 63B and training tokens should be 1.4 trillion. In conclusion, the application of the chinchilla scaling law in training large language models has provided a breakthrough in optimizing compute utilization and achieving efficient training. By recognizing the need to train models on longer time durations and a higher number of tokens, the chinchilla scaling law offers a compute-optimal approach that enhances the performance and capabilities of large language models.
